sections.h2: Who bills and who collects property tax in Wayne County?
sections.html:
Billing stays local. Each city or township in Wayne County builds its own assessment and tax rolls and sends the July and December bills through its own treasurer. The county enters the picture on March 1, when unpaid bills turn delinquent and become payable only to the Wayne County Treasurer's Office at 400 Monroe Street, 5th Floor, Detroit.

The county's Assessment and Equalization Division, part of the Department of Management and Budget at 500 Griswold, Suite 2650, advises the County Commission on equalizing local assessments and apportioning taxes. Its main line is (313) 967-0010. For Detroit, the county page points to the city's own assessor at (313) 224-3035 and the Detroit City Treasurer's Property Tax Division at (313) 224-3560.

Wayne is a charter county of about 1.77 million people, so the first call for a current bill is always the treasurer of the city or township where the house stands.

sections.h2: When do Wayne County property taxes become delinquent?
sections.html:
On the March 1 after the bill was due. Taxes unpaid to the local treasurer by the last day of February move to the county treasurer, and from then on payment is accepted only at the county. Every community and school district takes part in the Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund program, which the county describes as an alternate method of collecting delinquent property taxes.

The county treasurer's tax information line is (313) 224-5990. Delinquent payments can be made online, where bank debit is free and Visa, MasterCard or American Express carry a 2.49 percent service charge paid to the vendor. Partial payments are accepted by mail or in person, and an owner who wants a receipt should enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope.

The Treasurer's Office says it cannot waive interest or penalties, because state law holds the taxpayer responsible for paying on time. It also cannot lower a bill once issued. Relief for future years comes from exemptions, which the local assessor decides.

sections.h2: What is the forfeiture and foreclosure schedule in Wayne County?
sections.html:
Michigan's Public Act 123 of 1999 (MCL 211.78) cut the time before a tax foreclosure from about five years to about two. The county's timeline page lays out each stage, and the table summarizes it.

Wayne County Treasurer forfeiture and foreclosure steps under Public Act 123, by stage
StageWhat the county page says
First March 1 after the bill yearUnpaid taxes are delinquent and go to the county treasurer, with a 4% administration fee and 1% interest per month
October 1A $15 collection fee is added to each parcel
Following March 1The property is forfeited; $175 and $30 recording fees are added, and interest rises to 1.5% a month back to the first delinquency date
AutumnNotices of the show cause and judicial foreclosure hearings are served on an occupant or posted on the property
WinterRemote show cause hearings in January, then judicial foreclosure hearings in February
March 31Last day to redeem by paying taxes, interest, penalties and fees
April 1Foreclosure takes effect and title passes to the county treasurer
September and OctoberPublic auction of foreclosed parcels

The county says it sends at least ten notices, including four first class mailings, three certified notices, a personal visit and two mailings addressed to the occupant.

sections.h2: What help can a Wayne County owner get before foreclosure?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's Office runs payment plans and a hardship extension. The extension is for owners who hold title by recorded deed or land contract, live in the home as a principal residence and face substantial financial hardship. Its income standard is 125 percent of the Federal Poverty Level, though people just above it are told to apply anyway.

  • Bring a Michigan driver's license or state ID, a copy of the deed, proof of occupancy such as a utility bill, and proof of income.
  • Staff review the application and answer within 30 days of a complete submission.
  • Request an application at (313) 224-5990, by email at the taxpayer assistance address on the county page, or in person by appointment.
  • For title problems, the county lists United Community Housing Coalition at (313) 963-3310 and the Legal Aid and Defender Association at (313) 964-4130.

A poverty tax exemption, which can cut or erase future bills, is requested from the local assessing unit. Mortgage lenders also miss payments after refinances, so compare your statements with the local treasurer's records.

sections.h2: Can you sell a Wayne County house that has tax owing?
sections.html:
Yes, if the balance is paid through closing. A warranty deed needs county treasurer certificates showing no tax liens and that taxes were paid for the five years before the deed date, as MCL 211.135 requires. A quitclaim deed with no warranty covenants is exempt from that rule.

The county treasurer certifies deeds for $5.00 per document with up to 25 parcel numbers, then 20 cents for each parcel over 25. Only originals can be certified, either at the office by appointment or by mailing the originals with a check or money order to Wayne County Treasurer, Deed Certification, 400 Monroe St., 5th Floor, Detroit, MI 48226, along with a self-addressed stamped return envelope. After certification the deed goes to the Register of Deeds, where a separate appointment is needed to record it.

If the property is already forfeited, taxes remain payable until the following March, but interest keeps building each month. Settling the payoff at closing is simpler than waiting for foreclosure.

sections.h2: How do equalization and assessment appeals work in Wayne County?
sections.html:
Appeals begin locally. Valuation appeals go to the local Board of Review, then the Michigan Tax Tribunal. The county treasurer tells anyone granted a change through either one to ask the local assessor's office or the Tribunal to explain it.

County equalization is a second review of the totals. Under MCL 211.30a, each local unit delivers its roll to the county by the Wednesday after the first Monday in April. The Board of Commissioners then meets the Tuesday after the second Monday in April, and final county equalized values must be done by the first Monday in May under MCL 211.34. Its job is to spread the county's tax burden evenly among cities and townships.

sections.h2: What happens to a foreclosed Wayne County property?
sections.html:
The State of Michigan and local governments get the first chance to buy it for the minimum bid. Parcels not taken are sold at public auctions in September and October of the foreclosure year, starting at a minimum bid of the taxes, penalties and interest, and winning bidders receive a quit claim deed. Sales are "as is" and "where is".

Former owners may still collect leftover money. Under MCL 211.78t, a person who held title or equity when the property was foreclosed can file a notice of intent to claim any sale proceeds above the debt. It must be notarized and reach the treasurer by July 1 after the foreclosure. The treasurer answers by January 31, and a claimant may then file a motion in circuit court between February 1 and May 15.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Wayne County?
sections.html:
Wayne County is Michigan's most populous county, with 1,769,038 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate. Detroit is the seat and largest city, and the county includes Dearborn, Livonia, Westland, Taylor, Wyandotte and the Grosse Pointes. It covers 673 square miles, 9 percent of it water along the Detroit River and Lake St. Clair, and communities south of Detroit are called Downriver. Detroit Metropolitan Airport is in Romulus.

The Census Bureau lists 700,591 households, an owner-occupancy rate of 64.8 percent, a median owner-occupied value of $178,500, median household income of $60,539 and median gross rent of $1,132. Density is about 2,931 people per square mile, and values differ from one community to the next, so the local assessor's record matters more than a county average.

faqs.q: When do Wayne County property taxes go delinquent?
faqs.a: March 1. Taxes not paid to the local city or township treasurer by the last day of February become delinquent on the following March 1 and are payable only to the Wayne County Treasurer's Office.

faqs.q: How long before Wayne County can foreclose for unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: About two years. A year of delinquency leads to forfeiture the next March 1, and foreclosure follows after another year unless the taxes, interest and fees are paid by the March 31 deadline.

faqs.q: Can the Wayne County Treasurer reduce my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. Once taxes are billed the county cannot reduce them or waive interest and fees. Exemptions that lower future bills are requested from your local assessing unit.

faqs.q: What does Wayne County charge to certify a deed for taxes?
faqs.a: $5.00 per document with up to 25 parcel numbers, plus 20 cents for each parcel above 25. Only original documents can be certified.

faqs.q: Can I get money back if my Wayne County home sold at foreclosure auction?
faqs.a: Possibly. Owners with title or equity at foreclosure may file a notarized notice of intent to claim surplus proceeds by July 1 after the foreclosure. A court motion follows only if proceeds remain.
